source_batch.unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Facilities for Exporters and Importers

facts.statement: An exporter that could not realise export dues despite best efforts may self-write off or apply to the authorised dealer that handled the shipping documents. Limits: self-write-off 5% of the export proceeds realised in the preceding calendar year (10% for a status holder exporter); write-off by the authorised dealer 10%. The limits are cumulative. Conditions: the amount has been outstanding more than one year; satisfactory evidence of efforts to realise; the exporter has been a regular customer for at least six months, is compliant with KYC and anti-money laundering rules and the bank is satisfied of bona fides; and the case falls in a listed category: buyer insolvent with a liquidator's certificate, balance settled through an embassy or chamber of commerce, goods auctioned or destroyed by the authorities, buyer untraceable, undrawn balance of up to 10% of invoice value, legal action disproportionate to the amount, or bills drawn for the difference between letter of credit value and actual value or between provisional and actual freight and dishonoured. For the first three categories the bank may write off without limit. Proportionate export incentives must be surrendered, and a chartered accountant's certificate is needed for self-write-off.
facts.locator: Part C, C.23.1 to C.23.6; S03 printed p. 134

facts.statement: Cases that do not qualify for write-off: exports to countries with externalisation problems where the buyer has deposited the value in local currency but it cannot be repatriated; EDF or SOFTEX under investigation by agencies such as the Enforcement Directorate, DRI or CBI; and bills that are the subject of a civil or criminal suit. The bank reports write-offs in EDPMS.

Authorised dealers may allow set-off of outstanding export receivables against outstanding import payables with the same overseas buyer or supplier, or with overseas group or associate companies through a centralised settlement arrangement, on conditions including: operated through one authorised dealer; bona fides and no KYC, AML or CFT concerns; transactions not under investigation; ACU transactions kept outside; goods and services not set off against each other; balances outstanding at the time of set-off and the export and import legs in the same calendar year; a verifiable agreement or mutual consent (a written enforceable agreement for group settlement); no tax evasion; and each export and import transaction reported separately on a gross basis. The courseware adds that the EDF is released only after the entire export proceeds have been adjusted.
facts.locator: Part C, C.26.1; S03 printed p. 136

facts.statement: The EEFC account is held with an authorised dealer only as a non-interest-bearing current account. All categories of foreign exchange earners may credit 100% of their foreign exchange earnings; the sum of accruals in a calendar month must be converted into rupees on or before the last day of the succeeding calendar month, after adjusting approved utilisation and forward commitments. The facility is meant to save conversion costs, not to hold assets in foreign currency. No fund-based or non-fund-based credit may be given against balances in EEFC accounts. Resident individuals may include resident close relatives as joint holders on a former or survivor basis.
facts.locator: Part A, A.6; S03 printed p. 135

facts.statement: Firms and companies dealing in rough or polished diamonds or diamond-studded and precious metal jewellery, with a track record of at least three years and average annual turnover of Rs 3 crore or more in the preceding three licensing years, may transact through Diamond Dollar Accounts, up to five accounts with their banks. Participants in an international exhibition or trade fair may open a temporary foreign currency account abroad, and must repatriate the balance within one month of the close of the fair.
facts.locator: Part A, A.4 and A.5; S03 printed p. 135 says exporters with at least two years' track record; the Master Direction says three

facts.statement: Status holders may export freely exportable items (excluding gems and jewellery and articles of gold and precious metals) free of cost for export promotion up to 2% of average annual export realisation in the preceding three licensing years; for gems and jewellery and articles of gold and precious metals the limit is Rs one crore or 2%, whichever is lower; for supplies of pharmaceutical products, vaccines and life-saving drugs to health programmes of international agencies the limit is 8%. Exports not involving any foreign exchange transaction directly or indirectly need a waiver of the EDF procedure from RBI.
facts.locator: Part C, C.1; S03 printed pp. 135-136

facts.statement: Export finance is finance to exporters, framed by RBI to provide credit at internationally comparable interest rates. Pre-shipment finance (packing credit loan or export packing credit) is a working capital advance to procure, process or manufacture goods for export and to cover costs before shipment, such as packing, local transport and labour; it is liquidated from export proceeds, and the borrower normally needs a firm export order or an export letter of credit. Post-shipment finance (post-shipment credit) finances export bills after shipment. Pre-shipment finance can be export packing credit or an advance against government receivables such as duty drawback; post-shipment finance includes export bills purchased, discounted or negotiated, bills sent on collection, advances against consignment exports, advances against undrawn balances and advances against duty drawback.

Pre-sanction checks the courseware lists for an export packing credit: the borrower is the bank's customer and has an IEC; the exporter is not on RBI's caution list or ECGC's specific approval list; the exporter can execute the order in time; know-your-customer guidelines are complied with; the credit limit is commensurate with expected turnover; the period matches the manufacturing cycle. After sanction: no packing credit from another bank for the same order, stock statements, credit reports on foreign buyers, and liquidation of the packing credit from export bill proceeds, with the advance treated as a local advance at domestic penal rates if exports do not take place.

payload.title: Giving up on an export bill: the write-off limits and gates
payload.core_explanation_md:
When an overseas buyer will not or cannot pay, an exporter can **write off** the unrealised bill, subject to limits.

**How much (a share of export proceeds realised in the preceding calendar year)**
- **Self-write-off**: **5%**, or **10%** for a **status holder**.
- **Write-off by the authorised dealer**: **10%**.
- The limits are **cumulative**.

**The gates**: outstanding for **more than a year**; **evidence of every effort** to collect; a **regular customer** for **six months** and KYC compliant; **proportionate export incentives surrendered**; a **chartered accountant's certificate** for self-write-off.

**Which cases qualify**: buyer **insolvent** (liquidator's certificate), **settled through an embassy or chamber of commerce**, goods **auctioned or destroyed** by authorities, buyer **untraceable**, an **undrawn balance** up to 10% of invoice value, legal action **out of proportion**, or a bill for a **letter-of-credit difference** that was dishonoured. For insolvency, settlement through an embassy or chamber, and goods auctioned or destroyed, the bank may write off **without limit**.

**Does not qualify**: exports to countries with **externalisation problems**, bills under **investigation** by the ED, DRI or CBI, or the subject of a **civil or criminal suit**. Write-offs are **reported in EDPMS**.

payload.title: Netting a customer's exports against its imports: the set-off rules
payload.core_explanation_md:
An exporter who is also an importer with the **same overseas party** may ask its bank to **set off** what it is owed against what it owes, instead of two payments crossing the world.

**Allowed**: with the **same overseas buyer/supplier**, or with **group or associate companies** through a centralised settlement arrangement.

**Conditions to check**
- **One authorised dealer** operates and supervises the arrangement.
- **No KYC, AML or CFT** concerns; transactions **not under investigation**.
- **ACU country** transactions stay **outside** it.
- **Goods against goods, services against services**: never goods against services.
- Both amounts **outstanding at the time**, and the export and import legs in the **same calendar year**.
- A **verifiable agreement** (a **written, enforceable** one for group settlement).
- **No tax avoidance**.
- Each transaction **reported separately, gross**.

The courseware adds: the **EDF is released only after the entire export proceeds have been adjusted**.

payload.title: Keeping foreign exchange earned: EEFC, trade-fair and diamond accounts
payload.core_explanation_md:
**EEFC account** (Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency)
- Only a **non-interest-bearing current account** with an authorised dealer.
- **100%** of foreign exchange earnings may be credited.
- Accruals in a calendar month must be **converted to rupees by the last day of the next month**, after approved uses and forward commitments.
- It is for **saving conversion costs**, not for **holding foreign currency assets**.
- **No credit**, fund-based or non-fund-based, against EEFC balances.
- A resident individual may add a **resident close relative** as joint holder (**former or survivor**).

**Trade fair account**: a **temporary** foreign currency account abroad; repatriate the balance **within one month** of the fair closing.

**Diamond Dollar Account**: for firms dealing in **diamonds and jewellery** with **three years' track record** and **average annual turnover of ₹3 crore** or more; **up to five** accounts.

payload.title: Sending goods free of cost: the EDF waiver
payload.core_explanation_md:
Normally every export needs an EDF. For **free-of-cost exports for export promotion**, a **status holder** can use an **EDF waiver** up to a yearly limit based on **average annual export realisation over the preceding three licensing years**:

- **2%** for most exporters.
- **Gems and jewellery, and articles of gold and precious metals**: **₹1 crore or 2%, whichever is lower**.
- **Pharmaceuticals, vaccines and life-saving drugs for health programmes of international agencies** (such as UN agencies, WHO-PAHO): up to **8%**.

Such free-of-cost supplies get **no duty drawback or other incentive**. Exports that involve **no foreign exchange transaction at all** need a **waiver from RBI**.

payload.title: Export finance in two stages: before and after the ship sails
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Before shipment: pre-shipment finance**
- Also called **packing credit** (PCL or EPC).
- A **working capital advance** to **buy, process or make** the goods and to pay **packing, local transport and labour**.
- The borrower normally needs a **firm export order or an export letter of credit**, and the loan is **repaid from the export proceeds**.
- Types: **export packing credit**, and **advances against government receivables** such as **duty drawback**.

**After shipment: post-shipment finance**
- Finance against the **export bills**.
- Types: bills **purchased, discounted or negotiated**; bills **sent on collection**; advances against **consignment** exports; against **undrawn balances**; against **duty drawback**.

Purpose of both: credit at **internationally comparable interest rates**, so exporters can compete.

payload.title: Before a bank sanctions packing credit: the checklist
How much can an exporter write off this year?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an exporter that is **not** a status holder realised export proceeds of ₹36,00,00,000 (₹36 crore) in the preceding calendar year. A second exporter, a status holder, realised ₹24,00,00,000 (₹24 crore). Each has qualifying unrealised bills outstanding for more than a year. What are the limits for self-write-off and for write-off by the bank?

worked_steps.description: Self-write-off limit, ordinary exporter: 5% of ₹36 crore.
Bank write-off limit for the same exporter: 10% of ₹36 crore.
Self-write-off limit, status holder: 10% of ₹24 crore.
Bank write-off limit for the status holder: 10% of ₹24 crore.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Ordinary exporter: self-write-off up to ₹1,80,00,000.00 and bank write-off up to ₹3,60,00,000.00. Status holder: ₹2,40,00,000.00 self and ₹2,40,00,000.00 by the bank (the limits are cumulative)

self_check.prompt_text: The buyer of the ordinary exporter is declared insolvent and a liquidator certifies there is no possibility of recovery. Is the exporter confined to these limits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: for an insolvent buyer, with the liquidator's certificate, the bank may write off without any limit.

payload.stem_md: A status holder exporter realised export proceeds of ₹24,00,00,000 in the preceding calendar year. What is the maximum amount, in rupees, that it can self-write-off (subject to the other conditions)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

worked_solution_steps.description: Apply 10% to the previous calendar year's realisations

payload.stem_md: Which of the following statements about the limits for write-off of unrealised export bills is correct?

options.text_md: Self-write-off is 10% for every exporter; the bank may write off 5%
options.explanation_md: The percentages are the other way round for the bank.

options.text_md: The limits are 25% for self-write-off and 10% for the bank
options.explanation_md: No such 25% limit applies.

options.text_md: Self-write-off is 5% of the previous calendar year's realisations, or 10% for a status holder; the bank may write off 10%
options.explanation_md: These are the stated limits.

options.text_md: There is no limit if the bill has been outstanding for more than a year
options.explanation_md: The limits apply, with unlimited write-off only in listed cases.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Self-write-off is 5% (10% for a status holder) of the realisations of the preceding calendar year; the bank may write off 10%; the limits are cumulative.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is a condition for set-off of export receivables against import payables?

options.text_md: Receivables for goods may be set off against payables for services
options.explanation_md: Goods are not set off against services.

options.text_md: Transactions with ACU countries must be included
options.explanation_md: ACU transactions are kept outside the arrangement.

options.text_md: Only a net figure need be reported, not each transaction
options.explanation_md: Each transaction is reported separately on a gross basis.

options.text_md: Goods receivables may not be set off against payables for services, and the legs must fall in the same calendar year
options.explanation_md: Both are stated conditions.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Set-off is not allowed between goods and services, requires both amounts to be outstanding with the legs in the same calendar year, and each transaction is reported gross.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about an EEFC account is correct?

options.text_md: It earns interest at the savings rate
options.explanation_md: It is non-interest-bearing.

options.text_md: It is a non-interest-bearing current account and no credit may be given against its balances
options.explanation_md: Both points are stated.

options.text_md: Balances may be pledged to obtain fund-based credit
options.explanation_md: No credit facilities against EEFC balances are permitted.

options.text_md: Accruals may be held for any length of time to keep assets in foreign currency
options.explanation_md: Accruals must be converted by the last day of the next month, after approved uses.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The EEFC account is a non-interest-bearing current account, with no credit against its balances, and monthly accruals are converted into rupees by the end of the next month after approved utilisation.

payload.stem_md: What annual limit applies to free-of-cost exports for export promotion by a status holder in gems and jewellery, as against other sectors?

options.text_md: Rs one crore or 2% of average annual realisation, whichever is lower, against 2% for other sectors
options.explanation_md: The limit for gems and jewellery is Rs one crore or 2 per cent of average annual realisation, whichever is lower, against 2 per cent for other sectors.

options.text_md: 8% of average annual realisation, against 2% for other sectors
options.explanation_md: Eight per cent is not the stated limit.

options.text_md: Rs one crore or 2%, whichever is higher
options.explanation_md: Whichever is higher is not the rule.

options.text_md: No limit for gems and jewellery
options.explanation_md: A limit does apply to gems and jewellery too.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The limit for gems and jewellery is Rs one crore or 2 per cent of average annual realisation, whichever is lower, against 2 per cent for other sectors.

options.text_md: Finance against export bills after shipment
options.explanation_md: That is post-shipment finance.

options.text_md: A guarantee issued by the importer's bank
options.explanation_md: That is not finance to the exporter before shipment.

options.text_md: A working capital advance to buy, process or make goods for export and to meet pre-shipment costs, repaid from the export proceeds
options.explanation_md: This is packing credit.

options.text_md: A loan to the importer for the purchase of imported goods
options.explanation_md: That is import finance.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Pre-shipment finance (packing credit) is a working capital advance for procuring, processing or manufacturing export goods and for pre-shipment costs, liquidated from export proceeds.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is a form of post-shipment finance?

options.text_md: Export packing credit
options.explanation_md: This is pre-shipment finance.

options.text_md: An advance against raw material before an order is received
options.explanation_md: This is not post-shipment finance.

options.text_md: A running account for manufacture
options.explanation_md: That is a pre-shipment facility.

options.text_md: Export bills purchased, discounted or negotiated
options.explanation_md: These are post-shipment advances against export bills.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Post-shipment finance includes export bills purchased, discounted or negotiated, bills on collection, and advances against consignment exports, undrawn balances and duty drawback.

payload.stem_md: A packing credit was given for an export order, but the export did not take place. How is the advance treated?

options.text_md: As a concessional pre-shipment advance for another 180 days
options.explanation_md: The concession lapses if exports do not take place.

options.text_md: As a local advance, with interest at domestic penal rates
options.explanation_md: This is the treatment stated.

options.text_md: It is written off automatically
options.explanation_md: There is no automatic write-off.

options.text_md: It is converted into a post-shipment advance
options.explanation_md: There are no export bills to convert it into.

payload.correct_explanation_md: If exports do not take place after packing credit is allowed, the advance is treated as a local advance and interest at domestic penal rates is charged.

payload.stem_md: What is the track record and turnover test for a firm to deal through Diamond Dollar Accounts, according to the Master Direction?

options.text_md: At least two years' track record and any turnover
options.explanation_md: Two years was in the courseware; the Master Direction says three.

options.text_md: At least five years' track record and Rs 1 crore turnover
options.explanation_md: Those figures are not stated.

options.text_md: At least three years' track record and average annual turnover of Rs 3 crore or more in the preceding three licensing years
options.explanation_md: These are the conditions stated.

options.text_md: No track record if an EEFC account is held
options.explanation_md: Track record is required.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The Master Direction requires at least three years' track record and average annual turnover of Rs 3 crore or more in the preceding three licensing years; up to five accounts are allowed.

payload.stem_md: Which of these export bills qualifies for the write-off facility?

options.text_md: A bill where the overseas buyer has been declared insolvent and the official liquidator certifies no recovery is possible
options.explanation_md: Insolvency with a liquidator's certificate qualifies.

options.text_md: A bill where the buyer has paid in local currency which the central bank will not allow out
options.explanation_md: Externalisation-problem cases do not qualify.

options.text_md: A bill whose EDF is under investigation by the Enforcement Directorate
options.explanation_md: Investigated bills do not qualify.

options.text_md: A bill that is the subject of a civil suit in India
options.explanation_md: Bills under civil or criminal suit do not qualify.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A buyer's insolvency with a liquidator's certificate qualifies, and the bank may write off without limit; externalisation cases, investigated bills and bills in suit do not qualify.

unresolved: Export credit rules (periods of 180 and 360 days, the FOB deduction of 13-14% or 25%, interest rate linkage, running account, sub-supplier credit) on printed pp. 138-140 are not taught: RBI's export credit directions were being consolidated in 2025 and no current text was retrieved. The courseware's MCLR linkage (1 April 2016) is likely outdated.
The courseware's effective date of realisation of an export bill (printed p. 134) is a FEDAI rule, not retrieved, so not taught.
The courseware's statement that a Diamond Dollar Account needs a two-year track record (printed p. 135) differs from the Master Direction (three years); the Master Direction is taught.
The courseware's netting rule for SEZ units (printed p. 136) and the Master Direction's C.27 were not compared item by item and are not taught.
The courseware's EDF exemption list and gift limit of Rs 5 lakh (printed p. 136) are not taught.
RBI's Directions of 16 January 2026 (in force 1 October 2026) supersede the Export Master Direction; the substantive text was not retrieved.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.

items.stem_md: Which of the following statements about the limits for write-off of unrealised export bills is correct?

options.text_md: Self-write-off is 10% for every exporter; the bank may write off 5%
options.explanation_md: The percentages are the other way round for the bank.

options.text_md: The limits are 25% for self-write-off and 10% for the bank
options.explanation_md: No such 25% limit applies.

options.text_md: Self-write-off is 5% of the previous calendar year's realisations, or 10% for a status holder; the bank may write off 10%
options.explanation_md: These are the stated limits.

options.text_md: There is no limit if the bill has been outstanding for more than a year
options.explanation_md: The limits apply, with unlimited write-off only in listed cases.

items.correct_explanation_md: Self-write-off is 5% (10% for a status holder) of the realisations of the preceding calendar year; the bank may write off 10%; the limits are cumulative.

items.stem_md: Which of the following is a condition for set-off of export receivables against import payables?

options.text_md: Receivables for goods may be set off against payables for services
options.explanation_md: Goods are not set off against services.

options.text_md: Transactions with ACU countries must be included
options.explanation_md: ACU transactions are kept outside the arrangement.

options.text_md: Only a net figure need be reported, not each transaction
options.explanation_md: Each transaction is reported separately on a gross basis.

options.text_md: Goods receivables may not be set off against payables for services, and the legs must fall in the same calendar year
options.explanation_md: Both are stated conditions.

items.correct_explanation_md: Set-off is not allowed between goods and services, requires both amounts to be outstanding with the legs in the same calendar year, and each transaction is reported gross.

items.stem_md: Which statement about an EEFC account is correct?

options.text_md: It earns interest at the savings rate
options.explanation_md: It is non-interest-bearing.

options.text_md: It is a non-interest-bearing current account and no credit may be given against its balances
options.explanation_md: Both points are stated.

options.text_md: Balances may be pledged to obtain fund-based credit
options.explanation_md: No credit facilities against EEFC balances are permitted.

options.text_md: Accruals may be held for any length of time to keep assets in foreign currency
options.explanation_md: Accruals must be converted by the last day of the next month, after approved uses.

items.correct_explanation_md: The EEFC account is a non-interest-bearing current account, with no credit against its balances, and monthly accruals are converted into rupees by the end of the next month after approved utilisation.

items.stem_md: What annual limit applies to free-of-cost exports for export promotion by a status holder in gems and jewellery, as against other sectors?

options.text_md: Rs one crore or 2% of average annual realisation, whichever is lower, against 2% for other sectors
options.explanation_md: The limit for gems and jewellery is Rs one crore or 2 per cent of average annual realisation, whichever is lower, against 2 per cent for other sectors.

options.text_md: 8% of average annual realisation, against 2% for other sectors
options.explanation_md: Eight per cent is not the stated limit.

options.text_md: Rs one crore or 2%, whichever is higher
options.explanation_md: Whichever is higher is not the rule.

options.text_md: No limit for gems and jewellery
options.explanation_md: A limit does apply to gems and jewellery too.

items.correct_explanation_md: The limit for gems and jewellery is Rs one crore or 2 per cent of average annual realisation, whichever is lower, against 2 per cent for other sectors.

options.text_md: Finance against export bills after shipment
options.explanation_md: That is post-shipment finance.

options.text_md: A guarantee issued by the importer's bank
options.explanation_md: That is not finance to the exporter before shipment.

options.text_md: A working capital advance to buy, process or make goods for export and to meet pre-shipment costs, repaid from the export proceeds
options.explanation_md: This is packing credit.

options.text_md: A loan to the importer for the purchase of imported goods
options.explanation_md: That is import finance.

items.correct_explanation_md: Pre-shipment finance (packing credit) is a working capital advance for procuring, processing or manufacturing export goods and for pre-shipment costs, liquidated from export proceeds.

items.stem_md: Which of these is a form of post-shipment finance?

options.text_md: Export packing credit
options.explanation_md: This is pre-shipment finance.

options.text_md: An advance against raw material before an order is received
options.explanation_md: This is not post-shipment finance.

options.text_md: A running account for manufacture
options.explanation_md: That is a pre-shipment facility.

options.text_md: Export bills purchased, discounted or negotiated
options.explanation_md: These are post-shipment advances against export bills.

items.correct_explanation_md: Post-shipment finance includes export bills purchased, discounted or negotiated, bills on collection, and advances against consignment exports, undrawn balances and duty drawback.

items.stem_md: A packing credit was given for an export order, but the export did not take place. How is the advance treated?

options.text_md: As a concessional pre-shipment advance for another 180 days
options.explanation_md: The concession lapses if exports do not take place.

options.text_md: As a local advance, with interest at domestic penal rates
options.explanation_md: This is the treatment stated.

options.text_md: It is written off automatically
options.explanation_md: There is no automatic write-off.

options.text_md: It is converted into a post-shipment advance
options.explanation_md: There are no export bills to convert it into.

items.correct_explanation_md: If exports do not take place after packing credit is allowed, the advance is treated as a local advance and interest at domestic penal rates is charged.

items.stem_md: What is the track record and turnover test for a firm to deal through Diamond Dollar Accounts, according to the Master Direction?

options.text_md: At least two years' track record and any turnover
options.explanation_md: Two years was in the courseware; the Master Direction says three.

options.text_md: At least five years' track record and Rs 1 crore turnover
options.explanation_md: Those figures are not stated.

options.text_md: At least three years' track record and average annual turnover of Rs 3 crore or more in the preceding three licensing years
options.explanation_md: These are the conditions stated.

options.text_md: No track record if an EEFC account is held
options.explanation_md: Track record is required.

items.correct_explanation_md: The Master Direction requires at least three years' track record and average annual turnover of Rs 3 crore or more in the preceding three licensing years; up to five accounts are allowed.

items.stem_md: Which of these export bills qualifies for the write-off facility?

options.text_md: A bill where the overseas buyer has been declared insolvent and the official liquidator certifies no recovery is possible
options.explanation_md: Insolvency with a liquidator's certificate qualifies.

options.text_md: A bill where the buyer has paid in local currency which the central bank will not allow out
options.explanation_md: Externalisation-problem cases do not qualify.

options.text_md: A bill whose EDF is under investigation by the Enforcement Directorate
options.explanation_md: Investigated bills do not qualify.

options.text_md: A bill that is the subject of a civil suit in India
options.explanation_md: Bills under civil or criminal suit do not qualify.

items.correct_explanation_md: A buyer's insolvency with a liquidator's certificate qualifies, and the bank may write off without limit; externalisation cases, investigated bills and bills in suit do not qualify.
